slides.title: PHRASES MEANING EXAMPLE SING THE BLUES To feel sorrow or being sad about something You should not have sung the blues but looking for her. CRY OVER SPILLED MILK Being upset about something that happened and we cannot change Don’t cry over spilled milk, you gotta do something now. EAT SOMEONE'S HEART OUT To feel very sad or mentally pained It just ate my heart out to see her with someone else. COLD FEET Attitude that prevent someone to continue with the course of an action Rachel left Barry at the altar, she got cold feet at the last moment. EAT CROW To admit having been proven wrong after taking a strong position How does it feel to eat crow, John? LOSE ONE’S HEART To give up out of despair. To lament deeply I had already lost my heart waiting for an answer. RAW DEAL Unfair way of treating someone That was such a raw deal back there with Jen. SIT ON THE FENCE Lack of the ability to decide something I regret not making my mind up but sitting on the fence regarding Diane.

Language bricks

slides.title: We are able to express regrets in different ways. Check the chart.
visibleTexts: We are able to express regrets in different ways. Check the chart.

STRUCTURES STATEMENTS QUESTIONS N + Should Have + Past Participle I should have told them the truth before, What should you have done before? I shouldn’t have said those things. What should you have said? If only + N + Had + Past Participle If only she had acted differently, the story would be different. How would this have ended up if she had acted differently? If only I had expected nothing from them. I certainly look like an idiot now. Would you really have expected nothing from them? N + regret + V (ing) I regret calling her and letting her know about this. What do you regret? They did not regret making a scandal in front of everyone. Where they even sorry about that?

slides.title: To Consider 1. This structures do not necessarily work using the third conditional. 2. Should + Have + past participle is still used here. 3. We can use yes/no questions or Wh-words to go interrogative. 4. The context or the joining statements attached to these grammar structures are important and they need to be cohesive and logical. 5. All of them state a hypothetical or unreal situation in the past, EXCEPT regret + V(ing), that can be used in different tenses logically.

slides.title: We can use these structures to state the following functions:
visibleTexts: We can use these structures to state the following functions:

Functions Examples 1 Express life regrets I should have bought the car; now, I’m stuck here. 2 Lament on something If only they had listened to their parents, but they didn’t. 3. Regret one’s doings I regret inviting them so badly; they ruined our christmas party.

To consider We can also use - wish - to talk about things we want / wanted to be different. Present: I wish you did not live so far away. / I wish he’d stop talking. Past: They wish they hadn’t drunk so much. Now they are sick.

C. Read the following article and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read the text aloud to your teacher. You can read the full version on the link provided for further activities.

Regret can Seriously Damage your Mental Health There was once a banker in his 50s who had worked seven days a week for 25 years and become a very wealthy man. Then, at the apex of his career, he looked around him and realised that he had entirely neglected his family; as a result, his family had rejected him. The regret was overwhelming, and came out in panic attacks every Sunday. Would this man be able to find a way out of this cruel place he had created for himself? This man was a patient of the psychoanalyst David Morgan, of the Institute of Psychoanalysis, who spent several years helping him explore what had compelled him to work so hard and to ignore his children (he has been anonymised and gave Morgan permission to use his case). It became clear that this need to become richer than everyone else had roots in his very early childhood, when he watched his parents nearly starve to death during the 1980s miners’ strike. He had, unconsciously, repeated this by impoverishing his children by not being there for them, in turn impoverishing himself of these loving relationships, in his efforts to overcome the traumatic poverty of his childhood. “That complicated understanding,” Morgan explains, “freed things up, setting his regret in a generational context so he didn’t have to feel quite so guilty for acting something out, because it was beyond his ken. It doesn’t mean that he can’t feel real pain, but that pain is given a sense of history.” This meant his regret could be understood and given meaning – and that changed his life.

Regret can be all-consuming, and it can destroy lives. We can see it all around us, whether it is the man who cannot forgive himself for cheating on his first girlfriend and has not had a serious relationship in 30 years. Or the woman who is so tied up in wishing she’d had a child with her ex-partner, instead of breaking up with him, that she cannot find happiness in her current circumstances. It is not unusual for patients to seek therapy because they feel plagued by regret and unable to live full lives because of it, says Morgan, whether it is over affairs, career choices or relationships. The kind of regret that brings people to his consulting room is “paranoid and persecutory. It’s: ‘Oh God, I’m so terrible, I’m dreadful,’” he says. It is self-flagellation, and it can be incredibly damaging to our mental health. It is exhausting, it sucks all joy and fulfilment from our days and it leaves us stuck, always looking backwards and unable to move forward in our lives. The cognitive behaviour therapist Windy Dryden says that, when we are trapped in this cycle of regret, characterised by rigidity and inflexibility, we only seem able to blame ourselves for what has happened, rather than seeing our behaviour in a wider context and understanding why we took the path we did based on the information we had at the time. Under these conditions, regret will become toxic. Keep reading the article here: https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2019/jun/27/regret-can-seriously-damage-your-mental-health-heres-how-to-leave-it-behind
